name: Bilal Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an underground loader at a gold mine, the low, long machine that scoops broken rock out of the tunnels and tips it into the ore pass. We call it a bogger. Three days a week I'm underground at about 600 metres, and two days I run the same loader from a chair on the surface with joysticks and four camera screens. That's called tele-remote, and I was one of the first six people trained on it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Which do you prefer, underground or the chair upstairs?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, the chair, and the old hands give me grief for it. Upstairs I have coffee, I'm not breathing diesel, and I can run two machines across one shift while the blast fumes clear. Underground I like the crew and the noise, but my back feels it by Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, and I'd probably be a bit disappointed online, because I like this stuff. At work the older guys would say "told you so," and I'd let them have that one. It wouldn't change much in the lunch room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the path I'm on still works. Tele-remote loaders aren't hype; they already run here, and the mine wants more of them. So I'd keep being the young guy who knows the remote system, and that's a decent place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the remote operations ticket I'm halfway through, which is a licence for running gear from the surface. I'd keep using an AI chat app to quiz me on the course notes on the bus, like I do now. And I'd keep putting 300 a month into an index fund, which is a basket of shares, on top of the three months' costs I've got saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. I like change, so a world where nothing much happens is a little boring, but my rent gets paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI tools a lot. Where, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it every day: for the course, for my budget spreadsheet, and to fix the gaming PCs I build for mates on weekends. It's like a fast workmate who's sometimes confidently wrong. At work I don't use it much, because the loader doesn't care what a chatbot thinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are the money pressures that stay the same either way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, the car loan and sending my sister Nadia a bit for her nursing books. Gold's price is good right now, so the mine's busy, but I've seen it go quiet before. A plateau doesn't fix any of that, but none of it keeps me awake either.

say: I'd **accept it** calmly and let the older crew enjoy saying they told me so.
Online I'd be a little **disappointed**, because he enjoys new technology.
think: Tele-remote loaders are **real, not hype**, so his path at the mine still works.
Being the young guy who knows the **remote system** stays a good place to be.
do: Finish the **remote operations** ticket he's already halfway through.
Keep quizzing himself with an **AI chat app** on the bus to work.
Keep putting **300 a month** into an index fund on top of three months' savings.
feel: **Calm** and a bit flat, because he likes change and this picture has little.
S0.quote: Tele-remote loaders aren't hype; they already run here, and the mine wants more of them.
fieldNote: He separates **chatbot hype** from the remote machines that already work at his mine.
He uses AI daily **outside work** but barely on the loader itself.
His money pressures are **ordinary**: rent, a car loan and his sister's nursing books.

steps.text: Finish the remote operations ticket he's halfway through
Use an AI chat app to quiz himself on course notes
Put 300 a month into an index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where people like me do well, if we're honest about it. At work I'd tell the younger crew to get on the remote list now, not in three years. Online I'd probably post a video of the tele-remote setup, if the mine let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the thinking jobs around me get hit first: the planners, the people booking parts, the shift reports. My loader is hands-on, and underground robots spread slowly, so I've got time. And the remote chair is the bridge between the two, which is exactly where I'm sitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my supervisor, Kofi, to move me to four remote days a week within the year. I'd start an online certificate in mine automation and control systems, about 1,800 for the year, paid from my savings and hopefully half back from the mine. I'd learn whatever AI planning tool they bring in before anyone else touches it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly, with a little guilt. I know some of the guys I eat lunch with won't like where it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sione, who's 50 and the best underground operator I know, but he can't stand screens. He can feel a wheel spinning before the sensors can. I'd offer to sit with him on the simulator after shift, but I don't know if his pride would let him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the AI planning tool first. Would you want to bring it in, not just use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd want to be one of the people who sets it up. If they bring in software that plans the loader routes, I'd rather be the person who tells the software the drive at level 14 floods after rain than the person it replaces.

I'd tell the younger crew to get on the **remote list** now, not in three years.
think: The **thinking jobs** around him go first: planners, parts buyers, shift reports.
The **remote chair** is the bridge between hands-on and AI, and he's already in it.
do: Ask his supervisor for **four remote days** a week within the year.
Start an online **mine automation** certificate costing about 1,800.
Learn the mine's new **AI planning tool** before anyone else and help set it up.
feel: **Good**, with a little guilt about the lunch crew who won't like it.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the person who tells the software the drive at level 14 floods after rain than the person it replaces.
fieldNote: He sees himself on the **bridge** between hands-on mining and AI-run planning.
His worry is for others, like **Sione**, a skilled 50-year-old who dislikes screens.
He wants to **set up** the new tools, not just use them.

steps.text: Start an online mine automation and control certificate
Learn the mine's new AI planning tool before others
Help set up the loader route-planning software on his levels

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: this is huge, and the mine needs a plan for its people, not just its machines. Online I'd share it but I'd try not to sound like I'm cheering. Everyone would know I'm the tech guy, so they'd come to me with questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me more than I'd admit at work. If AI can do almost any thinking work by 2028, it can run the remote screens better than me, and the robots that make my hands-on skills useless show up around 2031. My remote chair isn't the safe spot I thought; it's just three years further down the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd look at jobs fixing the robots, not running them: maintenance technician, the person who swaps sensors and fixes hydraulics underground. I'd start a mechanical and electrical trade course this year, even if it cuts my hours. I'd pause the index fund and push my savings from three months toward six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jumpy. Excited by the tech and frightened of it at the same time, which is a strange mix to carry to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why fixing robots? Couldn't robots fix those too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots still break, especially underground where everything gets wet and smashed. My bet is someone has to crawl under them with a spanner for a long time after 2031. I'm not certain, though; nobody knows how good the repair robots get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister Nadia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Nadia to finish nursing, because people will still want a human holding their hand in hospital. I'd stop sending her money only if I really had to, and I'd tell her that straight. Family comes before the index fund.

say: I'd say the mine needs a **plan for people**, not just machines.
I'd share news online but try not to sound like I'm **cheering** it.
think: AGI by 2028 means AI could run the **remote screens** better than him.
His remote chair is only **three years** safer than the office jobs, not truly safe.
do: Look for **maintenance technician** roles fixing robots instead of running them.
Start a **mechanical and electrical** trade course this year, even with fewer hours.
Pause the index fund and grow savings from **three to six months**.
feel: **Jumpy**, excited by the technology and frightened by it at once.
S2.quote: My remote chair isn't the safe spot I thought; it's just three years further down the line.
fieldNote: The fast timeline **flips** his advantage: remote work is thinking work and goes first.
He bets on **repair work** underground but honestly admits he isn't certain.
He'd keep supporting his **sister's studies** before his own investments.

steps.text: Apply for robot maintenance technician roles at the mine
Start a mechanical and electrical trade course this year
Pause the index fund and build savings to six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to get this right, so the mine should start training people now. At the union meeting I'd back pushing for paid retraining. Online I'd be the guy posting course links.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is a sweet spot for me. AGI in 2031 takes the remote screens, robots around 2034 take the loader, and by then I can have a trade ticket and a few years fixing gear. I'd be 35, still young enough to start again if I have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the remote shifts for now and start the maintenance trade part-time next year, about two nights a week for three years. I'd keep the index fund going at 300 a month. And I'd talk to the maintenance superintendent about an internal move once I'm halfway through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a useful way. It gives me a deadline, and I work better with a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think most of your crew would do with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People will say the AI is coming, and then they'll wait to see the first robot before doing anything. By then, the training places at the college would be full. I'd rather be in a half-empty classroom in 2027 than queueing in 2032.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't moving back to hands-on work the opposite of what you've been doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I don't see it as either-or. I'd still use the AI tools on the remote screens until they don't need me, and learn the hands-on trade on the side. If it all slows down, I've just got two skills instead of one.

say: I'd say we have **five years**, so the mine should start training people now.
I'd back a **union push** for paid retraining and share course links online.
think: Five years is a **sweet spot**: AI takes the screens in 2031, robots the loader around 2034.
At 35 he'd have a **trade ticket** and still be young enough to restart.

Keep the **index fund** going at 300 a month.
Ask the maintenance superintendent about an **internal move** halfway through.
feel: **Uneasy** in a useful way, because a deadline helps him work.
S3.quote: I'd rather be in a half-empty classroom in 2027 than queueing in 2032.
fieldNote: He expects most crew to **wait for a robot** they can see, then crowd the college.

steps.text: Study a maintenance trade two nights a week for three years
Keep 300 a month going into the index fund
Ask the maintenance superintendent about an internal transfer
Vote for the union push for paid retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone who doesn't use it is choosing not to. I'd say it more kindly than that at work. Online I'd post about the courses and what they actually cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly good news. Robots for hands-on mining around 2039 means I've got over a decade of loader and remote work, and the AI before that probably makes my shifts easier. I'd be 40 when it really lands, with plenty of time to have moved twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and finish the automation certificate in the next year. I'd raise the index fund to 400 a month once the car loan's paid off in 2027. Then around 2030 I'd decide between the maintenance trade or a job designing the remote systems, depending on where the work is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. It's the version where I get to be early instead of lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could go wrong for you in the slow version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if I'm honest. I like the comfort of the chair. Ten years is long enough to get lazy, so I'd set myself a check every January. Am I still learning something new, or just coasting?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever start something of your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Possibly, yes. I've thought about it. A small business doing remote-system setup for smaller mines nearby that can't afford their own experts. But that's a 2032 idea, not a this-year idea.

say: I'd call ten years a **gift** and say not using it is a choice.
Online he'd post about **courses** and what they really cost.
think: Robots around 2039 give him **over a decade** of loader and remote work.
Earlier AI probably makes his **shifts easier** before anything gets taken.
do: Finish the **automation certificate** in the next year.
Raise index fund payments to **400 a month** once the car loan ends in 2027.

feel: **Calm** and a bit excited, because he gets to be early instead of lucky.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to get lazy, so I'd set myself a check every January.
fieldNote: He names his own risk, **coasting** in a comfortable chair, and sets a yearly check.
He floats a **small business** setting up remote systems for smaller mines, but later.
His long timeline brings **excitement**, not relief.

steps.text: Finish the mine automation certificate within the year
Raise index fund payments to 400 a month after 2027
Keep working tele-remote and underground loader shifts

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it turns my best card, the remote chair, into the first thing to go. What would help is the mine paying for trade courses and giving us time off for them, and some honest numbers on how many maintenance jobs they'll actually keep. Guessing is the worst part.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what the robots will be like to work next to. Nobody asks the operators what breaks, what floods, what jams, and we know. If they asked us now, the change would go better for everyone, the machines included.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks the operators what breaks, what floods, what jams, and we know.
portrait: Bilal is 27 and runs an underground **gold-mine loader**, three days below ground and two by tele-remote.
He's single, rents, has three months saved, and helps his **sister Nadia** with nursing costs.
He uses **AI tools daily** for study and his budget, and likes being early to new technology.
He feels secure in slow scenarios but sees fast AGI make his **remote chair** the first target.
His fallback is a **maintenance trade** fixing robots, which he admits is a bet, not a certainty.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it turns his remote-operator advantage into the first thing to go.
whatWouldHelp: The mine paying for **trade courses** and giving time off to attend them.
**Honest numbers** on how many maintenance jobs the mine will keep.
